titel: Yang Chu's Garden of Pleasure, by Liezi. Part II.

einzeiler: Philosophical reflections on fame, desire, and the art of living from Yang Chu.
kurzfassung: This episode explores the teachings of Yang Chu as recorded in the writings of Liezi. It contrasts the pursuit of empty fame and virtue with the genuine enjoyment of life and sensory pleasures. Furthermore, it examines mortality as the great equalizer that reduces all humans to the same dust regardless of status.
stichpunkte: Discussion on why people pursue fame and how it ultimately sacrifices reality for illusion
Comparison between real greatness tied to poverty and spurious greatness tied to wealth
Analysis of human lifespan, highlighting how little conscious time remains after sleep, illness, and anxiety
The inevitability of death as the great equalizer where intelligence and status dissolve into decay
Criticism of false virtues and extreme asceticism that lead to self-destruction
Comparison of different approaches to life, contrasting hedonistic indulgence with duty-bound governance
The philosophy of letting life and death take their course without anxiety over longevity or reputation
The four chimeras preventing peace: long life, reputation, rank, and riches

kapitel.titel: The Joyous Life of Tuan Mu Shu
The Folly of Desire for Long Life

clips.hook: Real greatness brings poverty, while spurious greatness brings wealth.
clips.text: Genuine greatness is characterized by a lack of material riches, whereas false greatness tends to accumulate wealth.

clips.hook: In life beings differ, but in death they share equal putrefaction.
clips.text: While living individuals exhibit vast differences in intellect and status, death reduces everyone equally to rotting remains.

clips.hook: Mental faculties give humans righteousness, propriety, glory, and rank.
clips.text: Human superiority over animals stems from mental capabilities that allow the attainment of proper conduct and social standing.

clips.hook: A single hair is a molecule of the body and must not be disregarded.
clips.text: Even the smallest part of the physical body holds importance because multiple hairs form skin and limbs.

clips.hook: Man must rely on intelligence rather than brute force.
clips.text: Lacking natural defenses like fur or sharp teeth, human survival depends entirely on intellectual capacity instead of physical strength.

beschreibung:
At the Court of Liang at the period of Yang Chu, about 300 B.C., the philosophers were treated as guests of the reigning king, who reserved for them lodging and maintenance, and encouraged all who had any pretence to the pursuit of truth and wisdom. Whether or not Yang Chu was actually a native of the Wei State, or whether he came there drawn by the attraction of a critical and unrivalled audience, it is at least certain that he settled there as small proprietor, probably in the reign of King Hwei, and continued there till his death, about 250 B.C.
One may imagine a condition of life in many respects somewhat analogous to the life of Epicurus in his famous Athenian Garden. To the philosopher of pleasure and contentment came pupils and disciples, discourses were held in much the same way as at an identical period discourses were held in the garden at Athens, and it is to these discourses, memorised and recorded by his favourite pupil Meng-sun-Yang, that we most probably owe the single fragment of the teaching of Yang Chu that remains, a fragment complete and explicit enough to enable us to form a clear estimate of his teaching and philosophy. - (from the Introduction by Hugh Cranmer-Byng)
Translated by Anton Forke.
